title: The deer in the hermitage
hookLine: hermits stop a king's arrow, and in their grove the deer don't run
carry: where non-harm takes root, hostility drops

lines: THIS DEER BELONGS TO THE HERMITAGE.
cards: A king is out hunting, standing in his chariot, an arrow already on the string. Ahead of him a deer runs for its life, glancing back over its shoulder. He's about to shoot when voices call out: king, stop!
This deer belongs to the hermitage. Hermits step into the path with their hands raised. And the king, the most powerful man in the forest, lowers his bow.
This is the opening of Kalidasa's play Shakuntala. As King Dushyanta walks on into the grove, he notices something strange: here, the deer don't run from the sound of his chariot.

teach.h: A GROVE WHERE DEER DON'T RUN.
teach.b: Hindu stories picture hermitages this way again and again: places where animals stop being afraid and hunters stop hunting. Patanjali puts that picture into one sutra.
Sutra 2.35: when someone is grounded in non-harm, hostility is given up in their presence. Not their own hostility. Everyone else's.
Grounded means firmly established, standing on it. The classical commentary says all creatures near such a person abandon their enmity. Then come the fruits of the other four restraints.
Grounded in truth, your words don't fail. Grounded in not stealing, jewels come near. Grounded in restraint, vigor.
Grounded in not grasping, insight into the how and why of your births. How should these be read? Within the tradition, some take them as real powers that come with mastery.

teach.h: POWERS, OR THE SHAPE OF A LIFE?
teach.b: Others read them as the natural shape of a life: people drop their guard around someone who will never hurt them, and trust the word of someone who never lies. Both readings agree on one thing.
The fruit doesn't come from chasing the fruit. The hermits didn't train the deer to be brave.

Their way of living did it, over years. You may have met someone like that: a grandmother who sits down at a dinner that's about to turn into a fight, asks someone about their garden, and the air changes.
She isn't performing calm. She stopped carrying a weapon a long time ago.

how: Hindu stories, from Kalidasa's Shakuntala to the Puranas, often describe hermitages as places where wild animals live at peace, and teachers of the Yoga Sutras present the fruits of 2.35–2.39 as signs that the restraints have taken root, whether read as powers or as the natural results of an ethical life.

o: the peace a person feels after forgiving a foe
a vow never to feel anger again, taken by sages
hostility given up around someone rooted in non-harm

games.q: each restraint and its fruit — tap the pairs.

s: 2.35 says the yogi stops feeling hostile
it says others give up hostility in that person's presence.
the sutra insists the fruits be read as literal powers
the sutra doesn't decide; readers within the tradition take them both ways.
in Kalidasa's play, the king lowers his bow at the hermitage
the hermits ask him not to kill a deer of the hermitage, and he does as they ask.

games.q: your dad and your uncle are one comment away from a fight at dinner. by 2.35, what actually calms a room like that?
o: the loudest voice telling everyone to stop.
pretending to be calm until it works.
a person firmly grounded in non-harm, not a lecture.
games.why: 2.35: hostility is given up in the presence of one grounded in ahimsa. it isn't performed; it grows from the restraint itself, like the hermitage where deer don't run.

practice: Picture the next room you'll walk into, a kitchen, an office, a group chat, and notice whether you're carrying anything sharp: a grievance, a comeback, a scorecard.
Set it down for the length of this sit, the way you'd leave a heavy bag by the door. Breathe as someone with nothing to defend.

wordCard.voice: Vaira-tyaga, the giving up of hostility that happens around one grounded in non-harm. The first of five fruits that come when the restraints are fully rooted.

orig.note: Sanskrit vaira-tyāga: vaira (hostility, enmity) plus tyāga (giving up); the fruit of non-harm in 2.35.

carryVoice: Your line: where non-harm takes root, hostility drops. The hermits never fought the king; their way of life lowered his bow. See you tomorrow.
